overview.title: Border effects and padding
overview.main_topic: Why an unpadded convolution shrinks the feature map (border effects), and how padding restores the input's spatial size.
overview.central_idea: A 3 × 3 window can only be centred on interior tiles, so a 5 × 5 input gives a 3 × 3 output (and 28 × 28 gives 26 × 26); adding one row/column of padding on every side (two for a 5 × 5 window) lets a centred window fit around every input tile, keeping the output size equal to the input size.
overview.importance: Explains the shapes in the MNIST model summary and the meaning of the padding="valid"/"same" argument introduced on the next page; essential for designing architectures whose shapes line up.
learning_objectives: Count valid window positions and compute the output size of an unpadded convolution.
Explain the border effect using figure 8.5 and the 28 -> 26 shrink in the MNIST model.
Describe padding and how many rows/columns are added for 3 × 3 and 5 × 5 windows.
Read figure 8.6: a padded 5 × 5 input yielding 25 patches.

summary:
**Border effects.** Take a 5 × 5 feature map (25 tiles). A 3 × 3 window must fit entirely inside the input, so it can be centred on only 9 tiles, the interior 3 × 3 grid (figure 8.5: the 5 × 5 grid with the central 3 × 3 shaded, next to the nine possible 3 × 3 patch placements). The output feature map is therefore 3 × 3: it shrinks by exactly two tiles along each dimension. This is the border effect already visible in the MNIST ConvNet, where 28 × 28 inputs become 26 × 26 after the first convolution layer.

**Padding.** To obtain an output with the same spatial dimensions as the input, use *padding*: add an appropriate number of rows and columns on each side of the input so that a centred window fits around every input tile. For a 3 × 3 window, add one column on the left, one on the right, one row at the top and one at the bottom. For a 5 × 5 window, add two rows (two on each side). Figure 8.6 shows a 5 × 5 input surrounded by a ring of padding tiles (drawn with crosses), making a 7 × 7 grid from which 25 3 × 3 patches can be extracted, one centred on each original tile; several of these patches are drawn, with their crossed padding tiles visible, followed by "etc."

The next page shows how this is configured in Keras (`padding="valid"` or `"same"`) and introduces strides.

paragraphs.what_it_says: In a 5 × 5 feature map only 9 tiles can serve as centres of a 3 × 3 window, forming a 3 × 3 grid (figure 8.5), so the output is 3 × 3: it shrinks by two tiles per dimension. The same border effect turns 28 × 28 MNIST inputs into 26 × 26 after the first conv layer.
paragraphs.what_it_means: Edge and corner tiles have no neighbours on one side, so a window centred on them would stick out of the input. Without padding, the window's centre must stay at least one tile from each edge (for a 3 × 3 window), losing one tile on each side, two in total per axis. In general, an unpadded k × k window on an n × n input gives an (n − k + 1) × (n − k + 1) output.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: Explains every spatial shrink in the MNIST model's conv layers (28→26, 13→11, 5→3) and why deep stacks of unpadded convolutions eat away at the borders.
paragraphs.technical_idea: $n_{out} = n_{in} - k + 1$ for stride 1, no padding.

paragraphs.excerpt: If you want to get an output feature map with the same
paragraphs.what_it_says: Padding adds rows and columns on each side of the input so that centred windows fit around every input tile, giving an output of the same spatial size. For a 3 × 3 window, add one column left and right and one row top and bottom; for a 5 × 5 window, add two (figure 8.6).
paragraphs.what_it_means: For an odd window size k, add (k − 1)/2 rows/columns on each side: 1 for k = 3, 2 for k = 5. The padded input is (n + k − 1) wide, and n + k − 1 − k + 1 = n, so the output size equals the input size. The padding values are typically zeros (Keras pads with zeros; not stated on this page).
paragraphs.why_it_matters: Same-size outputs make it easy to stack many conv layers without the feature map vanishing, and are needed for architectures like residual connections where shapes must match (beyond this page).

concepts.name: Border effect
concepts.definition: Shrinking of the output feature map because a window cannot be centred on tiles near the border without padding.
concepts.intuition: The stamp hangs off the edge of the paper, so you can't press it there.
concepts.technical: For window size k and stride 1 without padding: $n_{out} = n_{in} - k + 1$.
concepts.significance: Explains 28 × 28 -> 26 × 26 in the MNIST model and limits how many unpadded layers you can stack.
concepts.misconception: The shrink is not caused by pooling; it happens in the conv layer itself.

concepts.name: Padding
concepts.definition: Adding rows and columns on each side of the input feature map so that centred windows fit around every input tile.
concepts.intuition: Extend the paper with a blank margin so the stamp fits at the edges.
concepts.technical: For odd k, pad (k − 1)/2 on each side: 1 for 3 × 3, 2 for 5 × 5. Output size then equals input size (stride 1). Keras pads with zeros.
concepts.significance: Gives same-size outputs; corresponds to padding="same" in Keras (p.263).
concepts.example: A 5 × 5 input padded to 7 × 7 yields 25 3 × 3 patches (figure 8.6).
concepts.misconception: Padding does not invent useful content; padded tiles are just constant fill.

concepts.name: Convolution output size
concepts.definition: Number of window positions along each spatial axis.
concepts.intuition: Count the places a window fits.
concepts.technical: $n_{out} = n_{in} + 2p - k + 1$ for stride 1 (strides on p.263).
concepts.significance: Lets you predict every shape in a model summary.
concepts.misconception: Output size does not depend on the number of filters.

math.title: Output size of an unpadded convolution
math.source_text: There are only 9 tiles around which you can center a 3 × 3 window, forming a 3 × 3 grid ... It shrinks a little: by exactly two tiles alongside each dimension
math.operations: Count the starting positions 0, 1, ..., n_in − k of a window along an axis.
math.purpose: Quantifies the border effect described in the text.
math.interpretation: The output loses k − 1 tiles per dimension: 2 for a 3 × 3 window.
math.intuition: The window's centre can't come within (k − 1)/2 tiles of either edge.
math.numerical_example: $5 - 3 + 1 = 3$ (figure 8.5: 9 patches). $28 - 3 + 1 = 26$ (first MNIST conv). For a 5 × 5 window on 28 × 28: $28 - 5 + 1 = 24$.

math.title: Padding needed to preserve size
math.source_text: For a 3 × 3 window, you add one column on the right, one column on the left, one row at the top, and one row at the bottom. For a 5 × 5 window, you add two rows
math.operations: Add p on each side of each spatial axis, then apply the unpadded formula.
math.purpose: Shows why the book's prescription (1 for 3 × 3, 2 for 5 × 5) keeps output size equal to input size.
math.interpretation: Padding exactly compensates the k − 1 tiles lost to the border effect.
math.intuition: Give every tile, including corners, a full neighbourhood.

deeper.title: Shrinkage accumulates
deeper.body: Beyond the book: stacking unpadded 3 × 3 convolutions removes 2 tiles per layer. On a 28 × 28 input, ten such layers (no pooling) would leave 8 × 8; thirteen layers would leave 2 × 2. Border tiles also get used by fewer windows (a corner pixel appears in just one 3 × 3 patch of a valid convolution, a central pixel in nine), so information near the edges has less influence. Padding addresses both issues.

deeper.title: Checking with Keras
deeper.body:
Beyond the book (the padding argument is introduced on p.263):

```python
import keras
from keras import layers
x = keras.Input(shape=(5, 5, 1))
print(layers.Conv2D(1, 3)(x).shape)                  # (None, 3, 3, 1)  figure 8.5
print(layers.Conv2D(1, 3, padding="same")(x).shape)  # (None, 5, 5, 1)  figure 8.6
print(layers.Conv2D(1, 5, padding="same")(x).shape)  # (None, 5, 5, 1)  two-tile padding
```

deeper.title: A frame around a picture
deeper.body: Padding is like putting a mat around a photo before scanning it with a small magnifier that must be centred on each photo pixel: the mat gives the magnifier somewhere to rest at the edges, though it shows nothing interesting itself.

misconceptions.claim: A 3 × 3 convolution on a 5 × 5 input produces a 5 × 5 output.
misconceptions.correction: That only happens with padding. Without padding there are just 9 valid centres, giving 3 × 3.

misconceptions.claim: For a 5 × 5 window you add one row of padding.
misconceptions.correction: You add two rows (and columns) on each side; in general (k − 1)/2 per side.

misconceptions.claim: The 28 → 26 shrink in the MNIST model comes from pooling.
misconceptions.correction: It is the border effect of the unpadded 3 × 3 convolution; pooling then halves 26 to 13.

takeaways: Without padding, a 3 × 3 window can only be centred on interior tiles: 5 × 5 → 3 × 3, 28 × 28 → 26 × 26.
The output shrinks by k − 1 tiles per dimension (two for 3 × 3): the border effect.
Padding adds rows/columns on each side so a centred window fits around every input tile.
Pad one per side for 3 × 3 windows, two per side for 5 × 5 windows, to keep output size equal to input size.
Figure 8.6: a padded 5 × 5 input yields 25 3 × 3 patches.

questions.question: What is the output spatial size of an unpadded 3 × 3 convolution (stride 1) on a 13 × 13 feature map? On a 5 × 5 window applied to 28 × 28?
questions.explanation: n − k + 1: 13 − 3 + 1 = 11 (matches the second MNIST conv on p.257); 28 − 5 + 1 = 24.

questions.question: How many valid 3 × 3 patch locations are there in a 5 × 5 input without padding?
questions.explanation: The window centre must be one of the interior 3 × 3 tiles (figure 8.5). 25 is the count with padding (figure 8.6); 16 would be for a 2 × 2 window; 3 is the output width, not the count.

questions.question: How many rows and columns of padding are needed on each side for a 5 × 5 window to preserve spatial size?
questions.explanation: The book says two rows; in general (k − 1)/2 = 2 for k = 5.

questions.question: Why does the output shrink by exactly two tiles per dimension with a 3 × 3 window?
questions.answer: A centred 3 × 3 window needs one neighbour on every side, so the first and last row and column cannot be centres: one tile is lost at each end of each axis.
questions.explanation: This is the border effect the page describes; padding supplies the missing neighbours.

questions.question: In figure 8.6, what do the tiles drawn with crosses represent?
options: Pixels that are masked by dropout
Tiles with zero activation in the output
questions.explanation: The figure shows the 5 × 5 input surrounded by a ring of padding tiles, giving a 7 × 7 grid from which 25 patches can be extracted. Dropout and strides are unrelated; the crossed tiles are on the input side.

questions.question: Using the shapes in the MNIST model summary, identify every place the border effect occurs and every place something else changes the size.
questions.answer: Border effect: 28→26, 13→11, 5→3 (each Conv2D). Max pooling: 26→13, 11→5 (halving with flooring).
questions.explanation: Each unpadded 3 × 3 conv loses 2; pooling (p.263) halves.

questions.question: Can you draw a 4 × 4 input and mark the valid centres of a 3 × 3 window, then say what padding would make the output 4 × 4?
questions.answer: Valid centres are the 2 × 2 interior tiles (output 2 × 2); padding one row/column on each side gives a 6 × 6 grid and a 4 × 4 output.
